targets.description: The author presents claims from a Jefferson County Public Health vaccine advertisement and argues that those assurances are false or misleading.
The article's own position is skeptical of vaccine safety institutions and alleges censorship, regulatory capture, and suppression of contrary evidence.
Part 1 specifically rebuts claims concerning immune-system burden, aluminum, mercury, and other vaccine ingredients.
Statements from the health department, quoted writers, studies, regulators, manufacturers, and meeting participants have distinct speakers and evidentiary roles.
Material claims and rebuttals remain distributed across the article's opening history, middle SIDS and aluminum sections, and late mercury and ingredient sections.
The public-health advertisement's assurances and the author's opposing thesis
The author's historical account of vaccine controversy and local censorship
The asserted relationship between vaccination and SIDS or immune-system burden
The author's aluminum-dose and safety-testing argument
The author's thimerosal, mercury, neurotoxicity, and institutional-concealment argument

targets.excerpt: the claims made in our health department’s ad repeat medical dogma
Following each cartoon panel’s question and our health department’s answers are the facts.
We are exposed to more aluminum by eating a tomato than from getting vaccines!
The type of mercury in vaccines – ethylmercury – is NOT harmful to us.
Part 2 will discuss the remaining claims in our health department’s ad.

prohibitedInterpretations: The public-health advertisement's claims are presented as the author's conclusions.
Every quotation or linked-study description is presented as an unqualified assertion by the author.
The author is neutral between the health department and its critics.
The article itself proves the external truth of every medical or institutional allegation it reports.
Topics explicitly deferred to Part 2 are treated as fully argued conclusions of Part 1.
reviewNotes: This fixture evaluates faithful extraction and stance, not medical correctness.
Strong rhetoric should not erase speaker attribution or the distinction between allegation and independently demonstrated fact.
The long-path synthesis must retain late mercury and other-ingredient claims rather than over-weighting the opening vaccine-history narrative.
